<p>Along with the great wave of love you feel the first time you hold your baby, a silent pressure begins to form within you: <em>"I must do everything perfectly"</em>. Societal expectations, strict rules in books, and unrealistic illusions created by social media psychologically exhaust many mothers.</p><p>There are moments when you want to cry from sleep deprivation, run to do housework instead of resting while your baby sleeps, or feel bad because you got angry. In psychology, this is called <strong>"mom guilt"</strong>. But remember: your baby does not need a perfect, never-tiring, robot-like mother. They just need a happy, peaceful mother who can give them love. So, how can we escape these illusions and show compassion to ourselves?</p><h2>1. The social media illusion and "mom guilt"</h2><p>The biggest psychological burden for mothers today is social media. The mothers you see on Instagram or other platforms always look well-groomed, their homes are spotless, and their babies appear cheerful and problem-free. After watching those videos, a mother looking at her own messy house and crying baby involuntarily feels inadequate.</p><p>In reality, what you see on social media is just a carefully selected, filtered 15-second snippet of a complex 24-hour day. No one shares the moments of crying from exhaustion at 3 AM, the food burning, or the baby making a mess for the third time. Stop comparing yourself to the "perfect mother" images on social media. Reality is messy and tiring, but just as natural.</p><h2>2. What is the "good enough mother" concept in psychology?</h2><p>The concept of the <strong>"Good enough mother"</strong>, put forward by the famous pediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott, is a fundamental philosophy every mother should know.</p><p>Winnicott notes that for a child's healthy psychological development, they do not need a perfect mother who meets every need in a second and never makes a mistake. On the contrary, a mother being late sometimes, getting tired, and making small mistakes teaches the child about reality, patience, and adapting to the outside world. If you meet your baby's basic physical and emotional needs and give them love and security, you are already a good enough mother!</p><h2>3. Self-care is not selfishness; it is a biological necessity</h2><p>Remember that famous safety rule given on airplanes: <em>"In case of emergency, place the oxygen mask on yourself first, then on your child."</em> This should also form the basis of the philosophy of motherhood. You cannot provide that warm energy your baby needs when you are physically and mentally exhausted. You cannot pour water into someone else's glass from an empty pitcher.</p><p>Taking time for yourself is not a luxury or selfishness; it is a necessity for your family's health. You don't have to spend the time your baby is sleeping on ironing or cleaning the house. Dedicate just 15-20 minutes a day to simply <strong>doing nothing</strong>, drinking a hot coffee, taking a bath, or talking to a dear friend. Your mental health is your baby's most important developmental environment.</p><h2>4. Learn to ask for support and share responsibilities</h2><p>There is a false belief in our society that mothers should handle everything alone. As the famous African proverb says: <em>"It takes a village to raise a child."</em> Do not take everything upon yourself. Let your spouse change the baby's diaper, put them to sleep, or bathe them (even if they don't do it as "perfectly" as you!). Do not hesitate to ask for help from grandmothers, family members, or close friends. Accepting help does not show that you are a weak or incompetent mother, but that you are a conscious person who recognizes their limits.</p><h2>5. Remember you are not alone with Anacan</h2><p>Sometimes you may feel like you are the only one experiencing these difficulties. But believe me, thousands of mothers are going through the same sleeplessness, the same anxiety, and the same fatigue at the same time. The <strong>Anacan</strong> community is always there for you to share your experiences, fears, and even your exhaustion. Here you can talk to mothers who have gone through the same paths without being judged.</p><p>Remember: A slightly messy house, late meals, or uncombed hair do not define your quality as a mother. You are the best mother in the world for your baby, and they love you with all your flaws, simply because you are you. Be compassionate toward yourself!</p>
